alignment.note: καί / ܘܟܕ / Cumque — the temporal conjunction; Greek joins the genitive absolute with simple καί, while Syriac ܘܟܕ and Latin Cumque both fold the conjunction and 'when' together.

Greek employs a genitive absolute (ἐμβαίνοντος αὐτοῦ, 'as he was embarking'), whereas Syriac ܣܠܩ and Latin ascenderet use finite/subjunctive verbs governed by the temporal conjunction; the explicit pronoun αὐτοῦ is absorbed into the verb morphology in both versions.

Greek expresses the goal with preposition + article + noun (εἰς τὸ πλοῖον); Syriac ܠܣܦܝܢܬܐ marks the same directional sense with the prefixed lamadh, and Latin navim uses a bare accusative of motion without a preposition, each idiomatically equivalent.

Greek uses the single imperfect παρεκάλει ('was begging'); Syriac renders this with periphrastic ܒܥܐ ܗܘܐ (perfect + auxiliary ܗܘܐ to convey durative past), while Latin splits the idea into inceptive cœpit ... deprecari ('began to beseech').
αὐτόν / ܡܢܗ / illum — the object of entreaty; Syriac ܡܢܗ uses the preposition 'from him' as the natural complement of ܒܥܐ.

Greek substantivises the participle (ὁ δαιμονισθείς, 'the one who had been demon-possessed'); Syriac uses the relative ܗܘ ܕܫܐܕܘܗܝ ('he whose demons'); Latin expands into a full relative clause qui a dæmonio vexatus fuerat — semantically equivalent constructions differing in syntactic weight.
Greek ἵνα and Latin ut introduce the purpose/content clause; Syriac lacks a separate conjunction here, the subordination being carried by the prefixed dalath on ܕܥܡܗ.
μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ / ܕܥܡܗ / cum illo — 'with him'; Syriac compresses preposition, suffix-pronoun and subordinating dalath into the single form ܕܥܡܗ.
ᾖ / ܢܗܘܐ / esset — the subjunctive of εἰμί ('that he might be'); all three render the volitive 'be with him.'
